I am an old farmer who has worked this land for forty years. I have seen good years and bad years, and I know what works in Quzhou. My family has three people, and my children work off-farm, so I mostly manage the fields myself with some hired help during busy seasons. I have well irrigation, which is my lifeline.

This year, I will divide my 15 mu sensibly. I will put **10 mu into the wheat-maize double-cropping system** because it is reliable and the grain merchants always come to the village to buy. The remaining **5 mu I will plant with cotton** because cotton prices have been a bit better lately, and I still have the experience to manage it, though it is more labor.

For the **winter wheat** on 10 mu, I will sow an improved variety like Jimai 22 in early October. I trust this seed—it has good resistance and yields steadily. I will do rotary tillage before sowing to break up the stubble and prepare a fine seedbed. I will apply about 18 kg of nitrogen per mu, 6 kg of phosphorus, and 4 kg of potassium, split between basal and topdressing. Wheat needs water at critical times, so I will irrigate four times: the overwintering water, the reviving water in spring, once at jointing, and once at the grain-filling stage. I expect about 550 kg per mu if the weather cooperates. I will spray pesticides about four times total—once for weeds and two or three times for aphids and diseases.

For **summer maize** on the same 10 mu, I will plant a hybrid like Denghai 605 immediately after the wheat harvest in mid-June. I have learned that no-tillage sowing works well here; it saves time, keeps moisture, and the maize sprouts quickly in the warm soil. I will apply around 16 kg nitrogen per mu, 5 kg phosphorus, and 4 kg potassium. Maize needs less irrigation than wheat in our summer rains, but I will water twice if the drought hits—especially at silking and grain filling. I spray about three times: herbicide once, and insecticide for armyworm and corn borer. With good management, I expect 650 kg per mu.

For **cotton** on 5 mu, I will plough the field in spring to loosen the soil and warm it up, then plant an improved cotton variety in April. Cotton is hungry for potassium, so I will give it 14 kg nitrogen, 5 kg phosphorus, and 8 kg potassium per mu. I will irrigate three times during the growing season, especially at flowering and boll-setting. Cotton bollworm is always a threat here, so I must stay vigilant—I will spray pesticides about seven times across the season, including herbicide, insecticide, and a bit of fungicide. I expect around 250 kg of seed cotton per mu.

This is my plan. I know these fields like the back of my hand.
